paragraphs: A blank sheet. A few drops. A hidden message appears. What changed?

At a school science fair on National Science Day, 28 February, Ashwin and Keerthi receive sheets that seem to be blank. A volunteer wets the paper with a liquid, and a welcome message becomes visible. The children wonder whether the paper, the writing or the liquid explains the change.

At another stall, familiar substances produce different colours when mixed with plant extracts. These observations offer a way to investigate the mystery. You will compare substances, prepare indicators and use evidence to decide what a colour change can tell you.
Keep the message in mind as you work. By the end of the chapter, you will be able to suggest a possible explanation and a safe way to check it.

lesson.text: 2.1  Nature as a Science Laboratory

A liquid can look colourless without being water. Colour, smell and familiarity do not tell us whether it is safe. In this chapter, use only small amounts of samples selected and diluted by your teacher. Wear eye protection, protect the work surface and wash your hands afterwards. Never taste a test sample or touch it to identify its nature.
lesson.correction: Replace tasting and rubbing samples with safe observations and recalled food experience.

lesson.text: Compare both colours of litmus

Blue and red litmus papers let us compare a sample in two ways. Before testing, look at unused pieces of both papers. Will every liquid affect them in the same way? Record what happens before assigning the samples to a group.

lesson.figureCaption: Start with unused red and blue papers. Use a fresh piece for each drop.
paragraphs: Test teacher-prepared lemon juice, soap solution, amla juice, tamarind water, vinegar, baking soda solution, lime water, tap water, washing powder solution, sugar solution and salt solution. Include one other sample only with approval.
1. Place separate small pieces of blue and red litmus on a clean, dry white tile. Label the positions so you can identify each sample.
2. Put one drop of a sample on one blue piece and one red piece. Use separate droppers, or clean and rinse the dropper between samples.
3. Compare each piece with unused paper. Record both final colours in your notebook. Repeat for every sample; record unclear changes as unclear.
Keep samples away from eyes and mouths. Your teacher handles lime water and washing powder solution. Do not test cleaners, bleach or unknown liquids from home.

lesson.caption: Table 2.1  Record observations before classifying
lesson.note: Notebook record guide, not a table of results. Read across to pair the two observations for one sample; compare down to find patterns.

lesson.text: **Lime water** is a solution of calcium hydroxide in water. It is not juice from the lime fruit. A teacher can prepare it using suitable laboratory materials and separate the clear liquid from undissolved solid. Do not mix quicklime with water yourself: the process releases considerable heat and can splash an irritating mixture.
lesson.correction: Retain the chemical identity; replace student quicklime preparation with a teacher-only preparation note.

lesson.caption: Group samples by both litmus observations
rows: blue paper turns red; red paper remains red.
red paper turns blue; blue paper remains blue.
neither paper shows a clear change.

items: Group A: blue paper turns red; red paper remains red.
Group B: red paper turns blue; blue paper remains blue.
Group C: neither paper shows a clear change.

lesson.editorialRevision: 2026-09: concept distinctions presented as aligned comparison tables

lesson.text: Make three lists headed A, B and C in your notebook, using the three observed patterns. Put each sample in the list supported by both tests. Keep doubtful results separate for retesting rather than forcing them into a group.
lesson.addition: Bound uncertain observations and avoid pre-filled student results.

lesson.text: Suppose two groups test the same soap solution and report different colours. Check whether the papers began with the same colour, whether a dropper carried over another sample and whether the paper was wet already. Test fresh pieces using the same solution. Keep the first observations in the record as well as the repeat; crossing out an inconvenient result would hide the reason for checking it.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to sort-record

lesson.text: From observations to names

An **acid-base indicator** changes colour in response to the acidic or basic nature of a solution. Litmus is made from dyes obtained from certain lichens and is supplied as a solution or as paper strips. Some other indicators come from plants; synthetic indicators are manufactured. The indicator supplies evidence through its response; the original colour of the sample alone is not the test.

lesson.caption: Recognising acidic, basic and neutral samples
rows: lemon juice, amla juice, tamarind water and vinegar.
soap, baking soda, lime water and washing powder solutions.
pure water and suitable sugar or common salt solutions in pure water.
C, if neither paper changes; this is a limited test.

columns.title: Acidic
items: Evidence: blue litmus turns red.
Typical samples: lemon juice, amla juice, tamarind water and vinegar.
Classroom group: A.

columns.title: Basic
items: Evidence: red litmus turns blue.
Typical samples: soap, baking soda, lime water and washing powder solutions.
Classroom group: B.

columns.title: Neutral
items: Meaning: neither acidic nor basic.
Typical reference samples: pure water and suitable sugar or common salt solutions in pure water.
Classroom group: C, if neither paper changes; this is a limited test.

lesson.editorialRevision: 2026-09: concept distinctions presented as aligned comparison tables

lesson.text: Litmus does not measure an exact value of acidity. A very weak change can be hard to see, and a coloured sample can mask it. Tap water varies from place to place. “No clear change in either paper” is your observation; it does not prove that every water sample is exactly neutral or safe to drink.
lesson.correction: Qualify the source classification of tap water and distinguish observations from exact neutrality.

lesson.text: Consider two samples that leave blue litmus blue. One could be basic; another could be neutral. Blue paper alone has not separated them. Red paper adds a second comparison: a basic sample can turn it blue, while a neutral reference leaves it red. This is why a test that produces no visible change can still be informative when it is combined with another observation.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to neutral-limit

lesson.heading: A living source of colour
lesson.text: A lichen is a close association involving a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, usually an alga or a cyanobacterium. Look for lichens on bark or rocks without removing them. Different lichens tolerate different conditions, so finding one is not a complete test of air quality.
lesson.caption: Lichen growing on a small piece of bark.
lesson.correction: Extend the alga-only definition and avoid treating all lichens as proof of clean air.

lesson.text: Familiar foods, careful comparisons

paragraphs: Recall the taste of lemon, curd or tamarind that you have eaten as food. What do these familiar foods have in common? Do not taste the samples prepared for an investigation.

Some bases feel slippery and many taste bitter, but these are unsafe identification tests. Bitter gourd tastes bitter without being classified as a base. Explain why “bitter” is not enough evidence for “basic”.
Use a reference source to identify acids commonly present in lemon, curd, tamarind and vinegar. Compare your findings with the table below. A food can contain more than one acid.

lesson.caption: Table 2.2  Acids in familiar foods
rows: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and citric acid
lesson.note: Reference examples, not permission to taste laboratory samples. These names do not imply that a food contains only one acid.

lesson.text: An acid named in a food is one ingredient among many. A lemon is not a container of pure citric acid, and different fruits contain different amounts. Dilution changes how much acid is present in each drop. Do not rank foods by sourness in this investigation, or assume that an edible food makes every concentrated chemical with the same acid name safe to handle.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to food-table

lesson.text: Make an indicator from red roses

Can a flower supply a useful indicator? A coloured liquid obtained from a plant is an **extract**. Preparing the extract and testing it are separate tasks: first collect the colour, then compare its behaviour in known samples. Water carries some of the petal pigments into the liquid. Filtering removes petal pieces, which would otherwise make it harder to compare colours through the glass.

lesson.figureCaption: Washed petals, a mortar and a filtered extract. Let hot equipment cool.
paragraphs: 1. Collect a handful of fallen red rose petals, without plucking flowers. Use clean, suitable petals selected by your teacher; wash them with water.
2. Crush the petals with a mortar and pestle. Put them in a heat-resistant container.
3. Ask an adult to add enough hot water to cover the petals. Cover the container and wait 5–10 minutes. Let it cool before handling.
4. Filter the liquid into a clean container. The liquid that passes through is the filtrate. Keep some untreated extract for comparison.
Only an adult handles hot water. Label the extract; it is for testing, not drinking.

lesson.text: Describe the colour of the fresh extract before testing it. Petal variety, freshness and the amount of water can affect its appearance. An extract that is very pale or cloudy may give an unclear result. Checking it with known samples helps you decide whether it is useful.
lesson.addition: Explain preparation variability and a reference control.

lesson.text: During filtration, the paper holds back larger pieces while the coloured liquid passes through. The colour does not have to disappear for filtration to work: dissolved pigment can remain in the filtrate. Compare the filtered extract with the liquid containing petals. Which one gives a clearer view of a later colour change? This separates removing solid pieces from removing every substance in the liquid.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to extract-check

paragraphs: 1. Put the same amount of cooled red rose extract, about 10–20 drops, into three small transparent containers. Label them A, B and control.
2. Add about 20–30 drops of lemon juice to A and the same number of drops of soap solution to B. Keep the control unchanged. Use clean droppers.
3. Compare all three against white paper in the same light. Record the sample, the observed colour and the nature suggested by your earlier litmus test.
4. Test the remaining approved samples in fresh portions of extract. Keep the extract amount and sample amount alike across comparisons.
Do the samples that affected blue litmus show a similar rose-extract colour? What about samples that affected red litmus? Record disagreement rather than changing a result to match your prediction.

lesson.caption: Table 2.3  Read the rose test alongside the litmus test
rows: What you saw; compare with control
lesson.note: This is a recording guide. Compare down only after completing your own observations.

lesson.text: Imagine that a very dark fruit juice makes the mixture look red before the indicator has a clear effect. A red appearance alone would not show which material supplied that colour. Look at a small portion of the sample without indicator as well as the untreated extract. A separate litmus test provides another line of evidence. If the colour remains hard to interpret, record that limit instead of assigning a confident label.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to rose-guide

lesson.text: A suitable red rose extract commonly becomes a shade of red or pink in an acidic sample and green in a basic sample. A sample that gives little change needs comparison with the untreated extract and the litmus tests. The exact shade depends on the extract and sample: a printed colour is a guide, not a measurement.

lesson.caption: Illustrative comparison after testing: green, unchanged purple and red-pink. These are reference colours, not a record of your experiment.

lesson.text: Red hibiscus (gudhal), purple cabbage, jamun, beetroot and turmeric provide other colours to investigate. Do not assume that every coloured extract distinguishes acids and bases equally well. Compare each candidate with known acidic and basic samples and an untreated control.
lesson.correction: Present candidate plant pigments as indicators to validate, not equally reliable universal tests.

lesson.heading: Flower colour has more than one cause
lesson.text: Some hydrangeas produce blue flowers when acidic soil makes aluminium available to the plant. The same kinds may produce pink flowers when less aluminium is available. Variety matters too; white flowers do not simply turn blue. Soil conditions can affect colour, but a flower is not a substitute for a soil test.
lesson.caption: Blue and pink hydrangea flower heads.
lesson.correction: Add aluminium availability and cultivar limits to the source soil-colour claim.

lesson.text: A colour change inside a plant and a colour change in a test tube are related questions, but they are not identical tests. Roots take up substances, and flowers develop over time. Changing garden soil today will not instantly recolour every flower. To compare two plants fairly, consider their variety, growing conditions and the time of observation as well as the soil result.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to hydrangea

lesson.text: What can turmeric tell us?

Turmeric, or haldi, is a yellow spice from a plant in the ginger family. Its colour can be carried on paper. Unlike a two-colour litmus test, this indicator has a useful limitation: two different kinds of sample can give the same visible result. Keep a reference strip untreated so that drying, lighting or the original shade of the paper is not mistaken for a reaction to a sample.

lesson.figureCaption: Turmeric paste and unused yellow paper strips, ready for testing.
paragraphs: 1. Mix a spoonful of turmeric with a little water to make a paste. Fresh turmeric may be ground instead, with adult help.
2. Dip filter paper in the paste until it becomes yellow. Lift it out and let it dry. With adult supervision, cut it into strips.
3. Place a drop of each approved sample on a separate strip. Leave an unused strip beside them for comparison.
4. In your notebook, record the sample name and the final colour of its strip. Group samples with a similar result, then compare with your litmus groups.
Keep the paste and samples away from eyes and mouths. Use scissors carefully. Do not treat a missing colour change as a failed experiment; it may be evidence about the test.

lesson.text: Turmeric paper usually turns reddish-brown with a basic solution. It stays yellow with acidic and neutral solutions. It can therefore help identify a base, but an unchanged yellow strip cannot distinguish an acid from a neutral solution. Use both litmus papers to make that comparison.

paragraphs: Two samples leave turmeric paper yellow. One is vinegar and one is sugar solution. Can you decide which is which from that observation alone?
Choose another test and predict the two possible results. Explain why repeating only the turmeric test, even very carefully, would not supply the missing distinction.

lesson.text: An unchanged strip is useful only if the indicator is working. Use a small known basic reference chosen by your teacher to check a fresh piece of turmeric paper. If that reference also gives no clear change, investigate the paper or preparation before judging the unknown sample. A control does not provide the unknown answer; it checks whether the test can produce the response you are looking for.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to turmeric-think

lesson.text: A yellow curry stain may become reddish-brown when soap reaches it because the soap solution is basic. This links an everyday observation with the indicator test. Turmeric also has a long history of culinary and traditional use. Such use does not by itself establish that a preparation treats a disease; health claims need appropriate evidence.
lesson.correction: Retain the cultural context without asserting unproven health benefits.

lesson.text: Ashwin makes a greeting card for his teacher at Guru Purnima, writing in Odia. He coats paper with turmeric, lets it dry and uses a teacher-approved soap solution to write a message. Explain the colour he might see. Respect for a teacher can be expressed in any language; the chemistry of the indicator does not depend on the words.
An indicator detected by smell

Some substances show a change in detectable smell in acidic or basic conditions. They are called **olfactory indicators**. Smell is a less precise observation than it may seem: people differ in sensitivity, and repeatedly smelling the same substance can make it harder to notice. The sample’s own smell can also mask another smell. A control and a second kind of indicator help you avoid treating an uncertain impression as a definite identification.
lesson.addition: Bound the reliability of smell observations.

lesson.figureCaption: An onion container and three separate cotton strips. Keep a control strip.
paragraphs: This is a teacher-led demonstration using only approved food-based samples. Nobody is blindfolded. Do not participate in smelling if onion triggers discomfort or an allergy.
1. An adult chops onion and puts it with clean cotton or filter-paper strips in a closed container overnight.
2. Place three strips on separate clean surfaces. Keep one unchanged. Add a few drops of tamarind water to one and baking soda solution to another.
3. Only if your teacher approves, compare the smells by gently wafting air from a distance; never put a sample near your nose or inhale directly.
4. Record the smell before and after, including “no clear difference”. Compare with the unchanged strip. The teacher may repeat with other approved dilute samples.
Does your record distinguish the samples? If not, use a colour indicator. Never smell unknown laboratory chemicals or cleaning products.

lesson.text: The detectable onion smell may be reduced in basic conditions while remaining noticeable in acidic conditions. Results can be subtle with dilute baking soda. A weak smell, an unsuitable concentration or differences between observers can make the test inconclusive. It is not a way to identify arbitrary unknown liquids safely.
lesson.correction: Avoid promising a guaranteed smell result with dilute baking soda.

lesson.text: Suppose one observer notices less onion smell and another reports no difference. Record both descriptions. The amount of onion on each strip, the time allowed for the drops to spread and each person’s sensitivity may affect the comparison. Repeatedly taking a stronger sniff is not the solution. Discuss the uncertainty, then choose a safe colour test if the class needs clearer evidence.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to onion-explain

lesson.text: 2.2  When Acids and Bases Meet

An indicator reports the state of a mixture at the time you test it. If you add an acidic solution to a basic one, will the indicator keep its original colour? A drop-by-drop comparison helps you watch the change without assuming that equal volumes must balance each other. A concentrated solution contains more dissolved substance in a given volume than a dilute one. Similar-looking drops can therefore supply different amounts of the substances that react.

lesson.figureCaption: Teacher demonstration: a small test tube, dropper and clear solutions before mixing.
paragraphs: Your teacher performs this demonstration with eye protection, dilute prepared lime water and a stable test-tube rack. Do not prepare quicklime or mix household cleaners.
1. Put one drop of lemon juice and about twenty drops of water in a test tube. Observe its appearance; add a drop of blue litmus solution.
2. Record the colour. Add lime water one drop at a time, gently swirling after each drop. Record the sequence of colours and approximate drop count.
3. If the mixture becomes blue, stop adding lime water. Predict what adding lemon juice might do. Add one drop, mix and observe; if needed, continue a drop at a time.
Does one drop always reverse the colour? Compare your prediction with the record. The teacher disposes of the mixtures as directed for the materials used.

lesson.text: In **neutralisation**, an acid reacts with a base. For the acid and hydroxide base used here, the reaction forms a salt and water and releases heat. The amount used in this demonstration may be too small to make a temperature change easy to notice. A colour change alone does not measure heat.
lesson.correction: Bound acid-plus-base equation to the hydroxide case; no claim of perceptible warming in this tiny demonstration.

lesson.text: Acid + hydroxide base → salt + water
lesson.caption: Heat is released in this neutralisation. “Salt” names a family of substances, not only the common salt used in food.

lesson.text: Adding lime water reduces the acidic effect of the lemon juice. Enough added base can leave the mixture basic: blue litmus solution at the end is evidence of excess base, not proof of neutrality. Adding enough acid can make the mixture acidic again. The outcome depends on how much acid and base react, not just on equal numbers of drops.
lesson.correction: Correct the source equation of a blue endpoint with a neutral solution.

lesson.text: Think of each added drop as supplying another small amount of reactant. Early drops of base may react while acid is still left. Later drops may supply more base than the remaining acid can react with. Stirring matters because an unmixed drop can briefly create a local colour different from the rest of the liquid. Judge the well-mixed sample, and record the sequence rather than only its final colour.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to endpoint

paragraphs: One group says, “We mixed an acid with a base, so the result must be neutral.” Another says, “Our mixture turned blue, so some base is left.” Which statement uses the observation more carefully?
Explain why adding one drop of lemon juice might fail to reverse the colour. What information about the amounts and concentrations would help you predict the next change?

lesson.text: Prafulla Chandra Ray: research and education

Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray (1861–1944) was a chemist, teacher and industrial pioneer, often called the Father of Modern Indian Chemistry. After doctoral study in Britain, he returned to India and helped develop chemical research and teaching. His Bengal Chemical enterprise became a limited company in 1901. He also wrote about the history of chemistry in India and supported education through Indian languages.
lesson.correction: Use the company incorporation date precisely; omit unnecessary absolute first-company wording.

lesson.text: 2.3  Chemistry in Daily Life

A farmer notices poor growth. Is the soil too acidic, too basic, short of nutrients, too wet or affected by something else? Plant appearance alone does not identify the cause. Some fertilisers can make soil more acidic over time, but a soil test and knowledge of the crop should guide treatment.

lesson.caption: Compare a soil sample with a tested reference. Poor growth needs investigation before treatment.
Soil conditions and appropriate responses
rows: Soil too acidic for the crop
Soil too basic for the crop
a suitable soil test shows excessive acidity for that crop.
a soil test and crop needs identify the problem.
acidity alone does not explain the poor growth.
an expert may recommend a measured amount of agricultural lime.
seek local agricultural advice; suitable organic matter may help soil condition.
investigate nutrients, drainage, watering, pests and other conditions.
retest later; adding too much can create another problem.
compost is not a guaranteed or rapid cure for alkaline soil.
choose a treatment for the cause supported by evidence.

Response: an expert may recommend a measured amount of agricultural lime.
Check: retest later; adding too much can create another problem.

lesson.text: An ant bite is sometimes described as an acid-base problem. Some ants use formic acid in defence, but bites and stings differ between species. Skin reactions are not simply a beaker experiment. Tell an adult after a bite; wash the area with soap and water and use a wrapped cold compress. Do not apply test chemicals or baking-soda remedies. Seek urgent help for breathing difficulty or swelling of the mouth or throat.
lesson.correction: Replace blanket acid-neutralisation first aid with current NHS guidance; retain the example as a limit of the model.

lesson.text: Gurbir notices fewer fish in a lake near factories. Acidic waste is one possible cause, not a conclusion from the fish count alone. Oxygen shortage, toxic substances, temperature and other changes also matter. Treatment plants may adjust the acidity of wastewater before discharge, but a neutral reading does not prove the water is free of harmful substances. Treatment and testing belong with trained people, before waste enters the lake.
lesson.correction: Neutralisation is one treatment step, not proof of safe industrial discharge.

lesson.text: To investigate the lake responsibly, trained people would compare samples from suitable locations and times, including water away from the suspected discharge. Records before and after treatment would be more useful than one photograph. Students can discuss such evidence without collecting polluted water. Separating a possible explanation from a demonstrated cause is part of deciding what action could actually protect the fish.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to waste

lesson.text: Return to the hidden message

One explanation for the science-fair message is that a basic soap solution was used to write on the paper and allowed to dry. Wetting it with turmeric indicator would make the writing reddish-brown against yellow paper. Other indicator-and-solution pairs are possible. Suggest a prediction that would distinguish two explanations, rather than claiming that a colourful result proves one recipe.

Compare a patch written with soap solution with a patch wetted only with water. Let both dry, then apply the same indicator in the same way. If only the soap patch develops the predicted colour, the comparison supports the role of the writing liquid. If both patches change alike, examine the paper and indicator before claiming that the message has been explained.
lesson.addition: Focused evidence explanation linked to fair-explain

lesson.text: For a teacher-approved demonstration, test a tiny patch first and brush indicator onto paper instead of spraying it towards people. Use small quantities and keep food for eating separate from test materials. A visible message connects art and chemistry; a careful comparison explains why it appears.
lesson.addition: Use brush application to avoid aerosols; preserve the creative natural-indicator connection.

glossary.purpose: Reference definitions for terms taught in the chapter
entries: Acidic
A solution nature that can turn blue litmus red.
Basic
A solution nature that can turn red litmus blue; also called alkaline.
Neutral
Neither acidic nor basic; not a synonym for safe.
Indicator
A substance whose observable response helps identify a solution’s nature.
Extract
A preparation containing substances drawn out of a material, such as petals.
Filtrate
The liquid that passes through a filter.
Olfactory indicator
An indicator used through a change in detectable smell.
Neutralisation
A reaction in which an acid and a base react with one another.
Control
A comparison kept unchanged, or a known reference, used to interpret a test.
Lime water
A solution of calcium hydroxide in water, not a fruit juice.

summary: Use indicators and evidence to compare acidic, basic and neutral solutions. Never taste or touch test samples to identify them.
Acidic samples turn blue litmus red; basic samples turn red litmus blue. Use both papers and record unclear results.
Litmus comes from certain lichens. Plant extracts can also provide indicators, but their performance needs checking.
A suitable red rose extract commonly becomes red-pink in acidic samples and green in basic ones; compare with an untreated control.
Turmeric turns reddish-brown with a base. Remaining yellow does not distinguish an acidic sample from a neutral one.
Olfactory indicators involve a change in detectable smell. They require safe materials and may give inconclusive observations.
Neutralisation of an acid by a hydroxide base forms a salt and water and releases heat. An excess of either reactant can remain.
Soil and wastewater treatment require tests and suitable expertise. A neutral result does not mean a sample is safe.
A hidden-message demonstration uses a difference in indicator colour. Several recipes may explain the same visible result.

assessment.purpose: All twelve source questions retained with safety and evidence qualifications

questions.text: A solution turns red litmus blue. Which addition, in sufficient excess, could make the mixture acidic again? Choose lime water, baking soda solution, vinegar or common salt solution. Explain your choice.

Solution A turns red litmus blue; B turns turmeric reddish-brown; C turns a suitable red rose extract green. Which sequence describes A, B and C: acidic, acidic, acidic; neutral, basic, basic; basic, basic, acidic; or basic, basic, basic? Give the evidence for each.

Three containers tested with the same red rose extract give these colours: A green, B unchanged purple, C red-pink. Suggest the nature of each. For which container would another indicator be especially useful, and why?
questions.caption: A: green     B: unchanged purple     C: red-pink

questions.text: A sample leaves red litmus unchanged, turns blue litmus red and leaves turmeric yellow. Identify the nature supported by this evidence. Which observation is most useful, and why?

Manya cannot use a visual colour change in a teacher-led demonstration. Which kind of indicator might provide a smell-based comparison using approved samples? Explain its limits and precautions. Do not blindfold anyone or test unknown chemicals.

Suggest two possible pairs of writing liquid and revealing indicator for a hidden message. In your notebook, make a table naming each pair and the predicted colour. Explain how you would test the prediction safely.
Grape juice turns red rose extract reddish. Baking soda solution is added gradually. What changes might occur if enough is added? Explain why the starting amounts and concentrations matter.
Keerthi writes with orange juice and lets it dry. Suggest an indicator that could help reveal the acidic writing. Why would turmeric alone be a poor choice? Describe a control patch.
Describe how to prepare one natural indicator. State the materials, the safety precautions and how you would check that the preparation works.
You have vinegar, baking soda solution and sugar solution. What can unused turmeric paper identify directly, and what can it not distinguish? Suggest a further test.
Liquid X turns red rose extract green. What is its likely nature? Predict what sufficient excess amla juice might do to the colour, and explain your reasoning.

Reconstruct this decision map in your notebook: poor plant growth → test soil → compare the result with the crop’s needs → choose a response. Name a suitable indicator or soil test; describe responses for overly acidic and overly basic soil. Add a branch for soil near the required range.

projects.title: A different reaction
projects.text: Vinegar produces bubbles with eggshell or marble, while soap solution produces no clear bubbling. Both solids contain calcium carbonate. With your teacher, explain how an acid reacting with a carbonate can release carbon dioxide. Why is this not the same observable result as the lime-water neutralisation? Never seal a gas-producing mixture in a container.

projects.title: Colour, pattern and prediction
projects.text: Plan a small indicator rangoli on scrap paper using approved mild substances. Predict colours before applying drops or using a brush. Keep a record of each mixture, minimise waste and protect skin, eyes and surfaces. Compare the finished colours with your predictions.

projects.title: Compare local water safely
projects.text: With adult help, obtain safe samples of rainwater and tap water. A teacher may supply other samples; do not enter a river or collect polluted water. Compare them using indicators and a reference sample. Explain why the test cannot establish whether the water is drinkable.

projects.title: Investigate a local soil
projects.text: With permission, take a small soil sample without disturbing roots. Ask your teacher to prepare a water extract or use a suitable soil-testing kit. Record where it came from, the method and the result. Compare with the needs of a chosen plant; do not add treatments merely to change a colour. If comparing two sites, explain how you would keep the amounts of soil and water alike.
